courses.title: Closing Techniques
courses.description: 15 drills covering every core closing technique — direct, assumptive, alternative-choice, trial, silent, tie-down, takeaway, and re-close after an objection.

lessons.title: Direct Close
lessons.content:
Stop hinting. Ask directly. Every time.


WHY THIS WORKS

Most agents never actually ask for the sale. They present a quote, float a soft question, and hope the prospect volunteers a yes. That is not closing — that is wishing. A direct close is a clear, committed ask for the business immediately after your recommendation. It is not pushy. It is professional. Prospects respect agents who are decisive because indecision is contagious. If you are not sure about the close, they will not be sure about buying. This drill trains you to follow every single recommendation with one clean, direct commitment question — no trailing off, no softening, no 'no pressure though.'


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Make a clear recommendation using the prospect's own words.
2. Pause one full second. Let the recommendation land.
3. Ask directly for the business — one clean sentence.
4. Stop talking. Hold the silence. Wait for their response.
5. If yes — confirm details and move forward immediately.
6. If no — identify the objection and handle it before re-closing.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Based on what you told me — you want solid coverage, you have not had a claim in four years, and you are tired of overpaying — this policy is the right move for your household.
Agent: Let's get this started today. Do you want to go monthly or pay in full?
Prospect: Monthly works for me.
Agent: Perfect. I am pulling up your information right now. What is the best mailing address for your documents?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Asking 'How does that sound?' instead of asking for commitment
- Using the word 'maybe' — 'Would you maybe want to move forward?' kills urgency
- Presenting the quote and going silent waiting for them to decide
- Softening the close with 'No pressure though' which signals you do not believe in your own offer
- Asking multiple closing questions at once which confuses the prospect


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent has just presented a home and auto bundle quote to a prospect who called in from a warm lead. The prospect has been on the phone for 12 minutes, has given good discovery information, and the agent has just made a recommendation.

lessons.title: Assumptive Close
lessons.content:
Act like they already said yes. Most of the time they will.


WHY THIS WORKS

The assumptive close is one of the most powerful tools in insurance sales because it removes the moment of decision. Instead of asking 'Do you want to move forward?' you act as if the decision has already been made and move to the next logical step. This only works when you have done real discovery and made a genuine recommendation. If you try to assume the sale before earning it, prospects feel manipulated. But when used after solid rapport and discovery, the assumptive close feels natural — almost like you are just helping them complete a process they already started.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Complete discovery and summarize their needs back to them.
2. Make your recommendation with confidence.
3. Skip the ask and move directly to the next action step.
4. Use language that implies forward movement — 'Let me get that set up,' 'I will pull your documents now,' 'Your effective date will be...'
5. If they pump the brakes, stop and address the concern. Do not keep pushing forward.
6. Re-close once the concern is resolved.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Based on everything you have told me, this coverage makes the most sense for where you are right now.
Agent: Let me go ahead and get your effective date locked in. Is the first of the month better or would you prefer mid-month?
Prospect: Uh, first of the month I guess.
Agent: Perfect. And I will send your documents to the email we have on file — is that still correct?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Using the assumptive close before completing discovery — it feels like a trick
- Not stopping when the prospect pumps the brakes — pushes them away
- Using assumptive language in a weak, unsure tone — it only works with confidence
- Forgetting to confirm the next step clearly — leaves the sale in limbo


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent has done solid discovery on an inbound auto quote. The prospect is engaged, answered all questions, and the agent has just summarized their needs and presented a rate.

lessons.title: Alternative Choice Close
lessons.content:
Never ask yes or no. Give them a choice between two yeses.


WHY THIS WORKS

The alternative choice close eliminates the binary yes/no decision and replaces it with a choice between two options — both of which result in a sale. The psychology is simple: when people are given a choice, they focus on which option to pick rather than whether to pick at all. This close is most effective at the end of a call after you have presented options, but it can also be used at micro-decision points throughout the call to build a pattern of small commitments.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Present two clear options — different coverage levels, payment plans, or effective dates.
2. Make sure both options are genuinely good for the prospect.
3. Frame the question as a choice between the two, not as a yes or no.
4. Let them choose. Do not add a third option or walk them back to square one.
5. Confirm their choice and move forward immediately.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Both options work well for your situation. The question is whether you want the broader liability coverage with the bundle discount, or keep it to auto only and add home later.
Agent: Which direction makes more sense for you right now?
Prospect: Let's just do both together.
Agent: Smart move. Let me lock in the bundle rate right now.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Giving more than two options — too many choices cause paralysis
- Making one option clearly inferior — the prospect feels manipulated
- Using this close too early before the prospect understands their options
- Turning it into a yes/no by adding 'or would you rather not do anything today'


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An inbound prospect has been quoted on two options — auto only versus a home and auto bundle. They are interested but have not committed yet.

lessons.title: Urgency Close
lessons.content:
Real urgency closes calls. Fake urgency kills trust.


WHY THIS WORKS

The urgency close only works when the urgency is real. If you manufacture urgency — fake rate expirations, invented deadlines — prospects can smell it and you lose credibility instantly. Real urgency in insurance exists everywhere: rate holds expire, current policies lapse, life changes create coverage gaps, and rates increase when you delay. Your job is to find the real urgency in every call and surface it naturally. This drill trains you to identify genuine urgency and communicate it without pressure tactics.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Listen during discovery for real urgency triggers — lapse dates, life events, rate increases.
2. When you find one, note it and return to it at the close.
3. State the urgency factually, not dramatically.
4. Connect the urgency to their specific situation — not a generic 'rates are going up' speech.
5. Close immediately after stating the urgency. Do not let it hang in the air.


EXAMPLE

Agent: You mentioned your renewal is in 11 days. Once that renews you are locked in for another full year at that rate.
Agent: If we get this in place today, you are saving that money starting this month instead of waiting a year. It makes sense to move on it now.
Prospect: Yeah, you are right. Let's do it.
Agent: Let's get it done. I will have everything submitted before end of day.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Inventing urgency — 'This rate is only good until Friday' when it is not
- Stating urgency but not closing immediately after — the momentum dies
- Being dramatic instead of factual — 'You NEED to do this TODAY' sounds desperate
- Using urgency before you have established value — it just feels like pressure


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect called in for a home quote. During discovery the agent learned their current policy renews in 8 days and they are paying $400 more per year than necessary.

lessons.title: Summary Close
lessons.content:
Recap everything they said yes to. Then ask once.


WHY THIS WORKS

The summary close works by building a wall of agreement before the final ask. You recap every need the prospect confirmed, every problem they acknowledged, and every benefit they responded positively to — and then you ask for the business. By the time you get to the close, the prospect has mentally said yes a dozen times. The final ask feels like the obvious conclusion, not a new decision. This close is especially powerful on longer calls where a lot of ground has been covered.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Throughout the call, note every point the prospect agrees with.
2. Before closing, do a full recap: 'Here is what we covered today...'
3. Summarize their needs in their own words.
4. Summarize the solution and how it fits each need.
5. Ask for the commitment — one clean question.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Let me make sure I have this right. You want coverage that protects the home replacement cost, you want liability above the minimum, you need to stay under $180 a month, and you want one carrier for both home and auto. This policy checks every one of those boxes.
Agent: Does it make sense to lock this in today?
Prospect: Yeah, that covers everything I was looking for.
Agent: Perfect. Let's get your documents started.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Rushing the summary — it should feel thorough, not like a checklist
- Using your words instead of their words — loses the emotional connection
- Summarizing features instead of benefits tied to their needs
- Not closing after the summary — leaving it open for them to re-evaluate


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect has been on the phone for 18 minutes. Full discovery was done. They have a home, two cars, and a teenage driver. The agent is about to move to the close.

lessons.title: Silent Close
lessons.content:
After you ask — shut up. The first one to talk loses.


WHY THIS WORKS

The silent close is not a technique — it is discipline. After you ask for the sale, you stop talking. Most agents cannot hold the silence. They get nervous, start filling the gap, and accidentally talk the prospect out of saying yes. Silence creates pressure — healthy, natural pressure that allows the prospect to make a decision. If you break the silence before they do, you have just taken the pressure off and given them an exit. This drill is pure repetition of one skill: asking and then holding silence for as long as it takes.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Make your close — one clean sentence.
2. Stop talking the moment the question is out.
3. Do not clear your throat, add qualifiers, or restate the question.
4. Hold the silence. Count to ten in your head if you need to.
5. Let the prospect respond. Whatever they say — that is your next move.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Based on everything we covered, this is the right policy for your family. Are we moving forward today?
Prospect: ... ... ... Yeah, I think so. Let's do it.
Agent: Great. Let's get your information locked in.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Saying 'So... what do you think?' after the close — reopens the decision
- Adding 'It's totally fine if you need more time' — gives them an out
- Rephrasing the close because the silence made you nervous
- Laughing or making small talk to fill the dead air


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent has just delivered a clean direct close after a strong recommendation. This drill focuses entirely on what happens in the silence after the ask.

lessons.title: Tie-Down Close
lessons.content:
Build a chain of small yeses before the big one.


WHY THIS WORKS

A tie-down is a mini-commitment question embedded throughout the call — 'That makes sense, right?' or 'That is important to you, isn't it?' — that gets the prospect nodding along before you ever reach the final ask. Each small yes builds momentum and creates psychological consistency. When someone has said yes twelve times during a conversation, saying no at the end feels inconsistent with who they have been on that call. Used correctly, tie-downs make the close feel inevitable rather than abrupt.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Plant tie-downs throughout discovery: 'Having the right liability coverage matters to you, correct?'
2. Use tie-downs when presenting benefits: 'Saving $60 a month would make a difference, wouldn't it?'
3. Keep them short and natural — they should not feel like a quiz.
4. Build to the final close on the back of 5 to 8 confirmed agreements.
5. Close with confidence — the groundwork is already laid.


EXAMPLE

Agent: You mentioned you have not had a claim in six years — so you have been a low-risk customer for your current carrier, right?
Prospect: Yeah, exactly.
Agent: And they have not rewarded you with a lower rate for that, have they?
Prospect: Not really, no.
Agent: So a carrier that actually prices based on your record makes more sense for you. Let's get that set up today.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Using too many tie-downs — sounds like a script and feels manipulative
- Using tie-downs that are irrelevant to the close you are building toward
- Asking tie-downs in a singsong way — they need to sound natural
- Forgetting to close after building the chain of agreements


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An inbound prospect has called to shop their home insurance. They have been with the same carrier for 5 years and have not had a claim. The agent is mid-discovery.

lessons.title: Takeaway Close
lessons.content:
Pull it back and watch them lean in.


WHY THIS WORKS

The takeaway close works by triggering loss aversion — one of the most powerful forces in human decision-making. When people feel like something is being taken away from them, they want it more. Instead of pushing the prospect to buy, you introduce the possibility that they might not qualify, the rate might not be available, or the option might not be the right fit. Used ethically — meaning the concern you raise is real — this reframes the conversation entirely. The prospect shifts from being sold to to wanting to qualify.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Identify a real qualifier — underwriting requirements, rate locks, coverage eligibility.
2. After presenting the value, introduce the qualifier naturally.
3. Watch for the prospect to lean in — increased engagement, questions, urgency.
4. Confirm they meet the qualification and move forward.
5. Do not overuse this — it works once per call, maximum.


EXAMPLE

Agent: This rate is solid and it fits your situation well. The one thing I want to check is whether this carrier will accept your roof age — they are strict on anything over 15 years.
Prospect: My roof is 10 years old.
Agent: You are good then. Let's lock this in before the rate changes at the end of the month.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Manufacturing a fake qualifier — destroys trust if the prospect catches on
- Using the takeaway before establishing value — they do not want what they do not want yet
- Overdoing it — multiple takeaways in one call feels like games
- Not following through with the close after the takeaway lands


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect has been interested but slow-moving on a home insurance quote. The agent has built value and the prospect is engaged but not committing.

lessons.title: Trial Close
lessons.content:
Test the temperature before you commit to the ask.


WHY THIS WORKS

A trial close is a temperature check — a soft question that reveals where the prospect is in their decision-making without putting the full close on the table. It lets you know if you are ready to close or if you need to do more work first. The trial close protects you from closing too early and getting a hard no that is difficult to recover from. Think of it as reconnaissance before the main event.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. After presenting your recommendation, ask a trial close question.
2. Trial close examples: 'How does this compare to what you are paying now?' or 'Is this the kind of coverage you were looking for?'
3. Listen carefully to the answer — it tells you exactly where they are.
4. If positive — move directly to the close.
5. If uncertain — address the gap before closing.
6. If negative — go back to discovery and find what you missed.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Based on what we have put together — does this look like what you were hoping to find?
Prospect: Honestly yeah, the price is better than I expected.
Agent: Then let's make it official. Do you want to go monthly or pay the full year?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Using the trial close as a substitute for the real close — you still have to ask
- Not reading the response — getting a positive trial close and still not closing
- Asking a trial close that is too vague: 'So what do you think?' tells you nothing actionable
- Using trial closes too many times — the prospect feels like they are being tested


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent has presented a complete auto quote recommendation. The prospect has been listening but has not shown strong buying signals yet.

lessons.title: Re-Close After No
lessons.content:
No is not the end. It is the beginning of the real conversation.


WHY THIS WORKS

The first no is almost never a final no — it is almost always an unanswered question or an unresolved concern dressed up as a rejection. Top producers treat the first no as information, not as a verdict. The re-close formula is: acknowledge the no, isolate the real concern, answer it cleanly, and ask again. Most agents bail after the first no. That is why most agents are average. This drill trains you to stay in the call, handle the real objection, and ask again with full confidence.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. When the prospect says no, do not panic or apologize.
2. Acknowledge without validating: 'I understand' — not 'That makes total sense, sorry to bother you.'
3. Ask an isolating question: 'What specifically is holding you back right now?'
4. Listen fully. Do not interrupt or start forming your response while they are talking.
5. Answer the specific concern — not a generic objection script.
6. Re-close cleanly: 'Now that we have addressed that — does it make sense to move forward?'


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I just don't think right now is a good time.
Agent: I understand. Can I ask — is the timing the issue or is there something about the coverage or price that does not feel right?
Prospect: Honestly the price is a little higher than I wanted.
Agent: Got it. Let me show you the mid-tier option — it brings the monthly down by $40 and still hits your key coverage needs. Would that work better?
Prospect: Yeah that is more reasonable.
Agent: Then let's go with that. I will get it submitted right now.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Apologizing after the no — signals lack of confidence in your offer
- Re-closing on the same thing you already closed on — ignores the real objection
- Arguing with the objection instead of addressing it
- Giving up after one no — the data shows most sales happen after the third ask


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent made a clean close and the prospect said they are not ready right now. The agent needs to isolate the real concern and re-close.

lessons.title: Double Re-Close
lessons.content:
Handle two objections in a row and still get the sale.


WHY THIS WORKS

Some prospects give you a second objection after you have already handled the first one. This is normal — it does not mean they are not buying. It means they are still processing. The double re-close trains you to handle a second objection without frustration, without starting over, and without losing confidence. The key is to recognize the second objection as a buying signal — people who are truly not interested stop engaging. If they give you a second objection, they are still in the conversation.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Handle the first objection and re-close.
2. If a second objection comes, stay calm — recognize it as engagement.
3. Acknowledge the second objection briefly.
4. Answer it efficiently — you have already built rapport and established value.
5. Re-close for the second time with full confidence.
6. Do not apologize, do not restart, do not reduce the offer unless price is the real issue.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I still feel like I need to think about it.
Agent: What part do you want to think through? The coverage or the price?
Prospect: Both I guess. And I want to run it by my husband.
Agent: That is fair — let me ask you this. If your husband is fine with the price and the coverage, is there anything else that would hold you back?
Prospect: No, that is really it.
Agent: Then let's do this — let me get the application started now so you are not starting over when you talk to him. You can review it together tonight and I will call you in the morning to finalize. Fair enough?
Prospect: Yeah okay, that works.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Getting frustrated at the second objection — the prospect can hear it
- Treating the second objection as the final answer and giving up
- Going back to the beginning of the pitch — wastes their time and yours
- Matching their hesitation with your own — confidence is the only answer to hesitation


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent has already handled a price objection and re-closed. Now the prospect is giving a second objection about needing to speak with a spouse.

lessons.title: Either/Or Close
lessons.content:
Control the decision by controlling the options.


WHY THIS WORKS

The either/or close is a precision tool. It works by narrowing the prospect's focus to two specific decisions — effective date, payment method, coverage tier — so that the question is never 'should I buy' but always 'which one.' This close works best when you have earned the right to assume the sale through strong discovery and recommendation. Use it to drive commitment on a specific detail while the overall sale is assumed.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Confirm the recommendation has been made and received positively.
2. Identify a specific decision point — payment, start date, coverage level.
3. Present exactly two options — no more.
4. Ask the either/or question with a natural tone, not a salesperson tone.
5. Confirm their choice and move to the next step immediately.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Everything looks good on the underwriting side. Do you want to go with the first of the month or the fifteenth for your start date?
Prospect: First of the month works.
Agent: Perfect. And are you paying monthly or would you rather do the six-month pay?
Prospect: Monthly.
Agent: Done. Let me confirm your banking information and we will have you active before end of day.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Giving a third option when the prospect hesitates — defeats the purpose
- Using either/or before earning the assumptive sale — feels like a trick
- Making the two options unequal — the prospect will always pick the cheaper one, so know what you are offering
- Not moving forward after they choose — stalling kills momentum


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect has verbally agreed to move forward on a bundle quote. The agent is now in the binding process and needs to confirm key details.

lessons.title: Reverse Close
lessons.content:
Get them to sell themselves by asking the right question.


WHY THIS WORKS

The reverse close flips the dynamic. Instead of you selling the prospect, you ask the prospect to articulate why moving forward makes sense. When people say something out loud, they believe it more. When they say it in their own words, it becomes their idea. The reverse close is most powerful with analytical or skeptical prospects who resist being sold but will absolutely convince themselves if asked the right questions.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. After presenting your recommendation, ask an open-ended question about their own situation.
2. Let them talk. Do not interrupt.
3. Reflect their words back: 'So based on what you just said...'
4. Connect their words directly to the solution.
5. Close on their own logic.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Let me ask you something — what would it mean for your family if you had a claim and were underinsured?
Prospect: That would be a nightmare. We could not afford to rebuild out of pocket.
Agent: That is exactly why this coverage exists. Based on what you just told me — this is not really optional for your situation, is it?
Prospect: No, I guess it is not.
Agent: Then let's get it in place today.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Interrupting before the prospect finishes their thought — breaks the momentum
- Not connecting their answer back to the solution — the reverse close requires the loop to close
- Using this on prospects who are already sold — wastes time
- Overusing it — one powerful question is enough


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A skeptical prospect has been pushing back on price throughout the call. They have two kids and a home they own. The agent needs to get them to see the value in their own terms.

lessons.title: Puppy Dog Close
lessons.content:
Let them experience it before they commit.


WHY THIS WORKS

The puppy dog close gets its name from the idea that if you let someone take a puppy home for the weekend, they will never return it. In insurance, this means getting the prospect to experience the solution before full commitment — setting an effective date, running a soft credit pull, submitting a preliminary application. Once people have invested time and energy into the process, walking away becomes harder than moving forward. This close is especially effective with hesitant prospects who would buy if the friction of deciding was reduced.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Identify what low-commitment first step you can take that moves the sale forward.
2. Frame it as something you are doing for them, not something they are committing to.
3. Move them through the first step while they are still on the phone.
4. Build on each small step until the full commitment has been made incrementally.
5. Never misrepresent what they are committing to — that is where this technique goes wrong.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Let me go ahead and run your information through the system to see exactly what rate we can lock in. It does not commit you to anything — I just want to make sure I have accurate numbers for you before we make any decisions.
Prospect: Okay, sure.
Agent: Great. While I pull that up — is the address on file still current?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Using this as a trick to trap the prospect — they will feel manipulated when they realize it
- Not being transparent about what each step means
- Moving too fast through the steps and overwhelming the prospect
- Skipping the actual close at the end — the incremental steps are not the sale


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect has been interested but says they want to think about it before committing. The agent wants to keep them engaged and moving forward.

lessons.title: Ben Franklin Close
lessons.content:
Put it on paper. The math always wins.


WHY THIS WORKS

The Ben Franklin close involves walking the prospect through a verbal pros and cons analysis — or literally building one with them. It works because it shifts the conversation from emotion to logic, and the logical case for proper insurance coverage almost always wins. It also gives the prospect a sense of control — they are making the decision themselves rather than being told what to do. This is your go-to close for the analytical prospect who needs to think things through.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Ask the prospect if they are the kind of person who likes to make decisions by looking at the full picture.
2. Walk through the reasons to move forward — let them contribute to the list.
3. Walk through the reasons to wait — be honest and let them name the concerns.
4. Reflect the list back. The pros will almost always outweigh the cons.
5. Ask: 'Based on what we just laid out — what does the logical answer look like to you?'


EXAMPLE

Agent: Let's look at this simply. The reasons to move forward today: better coverage, lower rate, no lapse in protection, and you are done shopping. The reasons to wait: you want more time to think. Does the list tell you anything?
Prospect: When you put it that way, waiting does not really make sense.
Agent: It usually does not. Let's get it handled.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Stacking the pros and dismissing the cons — the prospect will feel railroaded
- Doing this for them instead of with them — it only works when they participate
- Using this on an emotional buyer — they do not want logic, they want connection
- Not closing after the analysis — the close still requires an ask


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A detail-oriented prospect has been asking lots of questions throughout the call. They have the information they need but cannot seem to make a decision.

courses.title: Objection Handling
courses.description: 20 drills for the objections producers hear every day — think-about-it, spouse, price, shop-around, already-have-an-agent, credit concerns, and more — each with the language to handle it and move the call forward.

lessons.title: Think About It
lessons.content:
What they mean is they do not have enough information yet.


WHY THIS WORKS

'I need to think about it' is the most common stall in sales and it almost never means what it sounds like. It rarely means 'I have all the information and just need time.' It almost always means one of three things: they do not fully understand what they are buying, they have a concern they have not voiced, or they do not see enough value to decide now. Your job is not to give them time to think — it is to find out which of those three things is true and address it directly.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Acknowledge without surrendering: 'I completely understand wanting to make a good decision.'
2. Isolate: 'Can I ask — is there a specific part you want to think through, or is it more of a general feeling?'
3. Listen. Let them tell you the real objection.
4. Address the real issue.
5. Re-close with a commitment question.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I just want to think about it a little more.
Agent: I understand wanting to be sure. Is there a specific part of the coverage or the price that you want to think through? Or is it something else?
Prospect: Honestly I just feel like I should get more quotes.
Agent: That makes sense. What I can tell you is that in three years of doing this, the agents who get you a better rate on this profile are rare — and you would be spending your time to get to the same place. But tell me what you were hoping to find, and I will tell you honestly whether it is out there.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Saying 'Of course, take all the time you need' — you just lost the sale
- Trying to rush them — creates resistance
- Not isolating the real objection before responding
- Giving a monologue about why they should decide now without listening first


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent has presented a full home and auto bundle quote. The prospect says they need to think about it.

lessons.title: Talk To Spouse / Partner
lessons.content:
Get the spouse on the call or get a committed next step.


WHY THIS WORKS

The spouse objection is legitimate — major financial decisions often do involve a partner. Your job is not to dismiss this but to work with it. The two options are: get the spouse on the call right now, or lock in a specific committed callback where both people are present. The worst outcome is agreeing to call back 'sometime' with no specific commitment. That call almost never happens.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Validate: 'That makes complete sense — this is a household decision.'
2. Attempt to get them on the call: 'Is your partner available right now? This will only take 10 minutes.'
3. If not available, lock in a specific callback: 'What time tonight works for both of you?'
4. Get the exact day, time, and confirm you have the right number.
5. Before hanging up, get a soft commitment: 'If the numbers look the same when we talk tonight, are you ready to move forward?'


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I really need to run this by my wife first.
Agent: Absolutely — is she available right now? I can walk her through it in about 10 minutes so you are both on the same page.
Prospect: She is at work right now.
Agent: No problem. What time tonight works for both of you? I will call you when you are both together.
Prospect: Around 7 works.
Agent: Perfect. I will call you at 7. And let me ask — if the numbers look the same when we talk tonight, is there anything that would hold you back?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Accepting 'I'll talk to them and call you back' — this never happens
- Not attempting to get the spouse on the call before scheduling a callback
- Scheduling a vague callback with no specific time
- Not getting a soft commitment before hanging up


PRACTICE SCENARIO

Mid-close, the prospect says they need to speak to their spouse before making a decision.

lessons.title: Send It Over
lessons.content:
Email is where deals go to die. Keep them on the phone.


WHY THIS WORKS

'Send it over' is almost always a polite way of ending the conversation. Once they have the email, you have lost control of the sale. They will either never open it, forward it to a competitor for a better rate, or use it as a comparison tool that removes your relationship advantage. The goal is to handle this objection before you get off the phone and convert to a committed next step.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Do not immediately say no to sending information.
2. Ask what specifically they want to review: 'What part do you want to look over?'
3. Address that specific part on the call.
4. If they still want something in writing, commit to sending it — but lock in a follow-up call at a specific time while they are still on the phone.
5. Use the follow-up call to close.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: Can you just send me something to look over?
Agent: Absolutely. What specifically do you want to review — the coverage breakdown or the pricing?
Prospect: Both I guess.
Agent: I can do that. Let me send it while we are on the phone and I will walk you through it in real time — that way if you have questions you do not have to track me down later. Does that work?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Agreeing to send it and hanging up with no follow-up plan
- Arguing with the objection: 'Email is not as helpful as talking' — they do not care
- Sending a wall of information that overwhelms instead of clarifies
- Not locking in a follow-up call before getting off the phone


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent has presented a quote. The prospect asks to have something sent to their email to look over.

lessons.title: Happy Where I'm At
lessons.content:
Happy is not the same as well-served.


WHY THIS WORKS

'I am happy with my current carrier' is not a no — it is an invitation to show them something better. Happy customers stay loyal out of inertia, not because they have compared their options. Your job is to create a moment of honest comparison without bashing their current carrier. If they knew what you know about their coverage and rate, they might not be so happy. This objection is handled through curiosity, not confrontation.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Respect the relationship: 'That is great — loyalty to a carrier you like is smart.'
2. Plant a seed of curiosity: 'Can I ask — when did you last actually compare your rate?'
3. Listen to their answer. More than 2 years = significant opportunity.
4. Request just five minutes to show them the comparison.
5. If the numbers are better — the sale makes itself.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I have been with State Farm for 10 years and I am pretty happy with them.
Agent: That is a good sign — it means you have not had any major issues. Let me ask you — when was the last time someone actually showed you what your coverage looks like line by line and whether the rate reflects your current risk profile?
Prospect: Honestly, never really.
Agent: That is more common than you think. It takes about five minutes. What I find most of the time is people are either getting a great deal and they should stay — or they are overpaying and they should not be. Either way you will know for sure. Want me to take a look?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Bashing the current carrier — creates defensiveness
- Immediately trying to sell before establishing the comparison
- Giving up when they say they are happy without exploring further
- Promising a better rate before you have run the numbers


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An inbound lead that was generated from a comparison shopping site. The prospect says they called but they are already happy with their current carrier.

lessons.title: Too Expensive / Price Objection
lessons.content:
Price is never the real objection. Value is.


WHY THIS WORKS

When a prospect says something is too expensive, they are almost never saying the dollar amount is literally outside their budget. They are saying the value they perceive does not justify the price they see. Your job is not to lower the price — it is to raise the perceived value. Start by understanding what they are comparing it to. Then rebuild the value case around what that coverage actually protects. Price objections collapse when value is crystal clear.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Do not immediately offer a discount or lower option.
2. Ask: 'Compared to what?' — find out the reference point.
3. If comparing to current carrier — do a line-by-line coverage comparison.
4. Rebuild value: what does this coverage protect? What would it cost them without it?
5. If price is genuinely too high — present a lower option, but do not abandon value framing.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: That seems really high compared to what I am paying now.
Agent: What are you paying currently?
Prospect: Around $90 a month.
Agent: Got it. Can I ask — do you know what your liability limits are on that policy?
Prospect: Not off the top of my head.
Agent: That is usually where the difference lives. A lot of carriers keep the premium low by dropping liability below what actually protects you. Let me show you what you are getting for $90 versus what you would have here.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Immediately lowering the price — trains them to object on price every time
- Getting defensive about the rate instead of addressing the value gap
- Not asking what they are comparing it to
- Agreeing that the price is high — never validate the price objection


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent has presented a full coverage auto quote. The prospect says it is more expensive than they expected.

lessons.title: Need To Shop Around
lessons.content:
You are the last stop they need to make.


WHY THIS WORKS

Shopping around is a rational thing to do with a major purchase. Acknowledge it. Then make the case — efficiently and factually — that continuing to shop is a use of their time that is unlikely to produce a meaningfully different result for their specific profile. The goal is not to stop them from comparing but to make them feel like comparing further is unnecessary because the comparison has already been done for them.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Validate: 'Shopping around is smart with something this important.'
2. Ask what they are looking for that they have not found yet.
3. Address that specific gap directly.
4. Make the case for why continuing to shop is unlikely to change the outcome.
5. Offer a contingency: 'If you find something significantly better, I want to know about it.'


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I want to get a few more quotes before I make a decision.
Agent: That makes sense. What are you hoping to find that you have not seen yet — better price, different coverage, something else?
Prospect: Just want to make sure I am getting the best deal.
Agent: I respect that. Here is what I can tell you — I have already run this against our top three carriers for your zip code and profile. The rate you have here is where the market is. You can spend two hours getting four more quotes and land in the same place, or we can get this locked in now. What would make you feel good about this?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Telling them not to shop — creates resistance
- Not finding out what they are actually looking for
- Being vague about why they do not need to shop further
- Letting them off the phone without a committed next step


PRACTICE SCENARIO

Near the close, the prospect says they want to get a few more quotes before committing.

lessons.title: Call Me Back Later
lessons.content:
Later without a time is never.


WHY THIS WORKS

'Call me back later' without a specific time is a polite way of saying goodbye. Never accept it without converting it to a real appointment. A real appointment has a specific day, specific time, and a soft commitment about what happens on that call. Your goal in this moment is to turn a vague dismissal into a genuine next step.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Do not say 'Sure, when is good?' — too open-ended.
2. Propose a specific time: 'Would tonight around 6 work or is tomorrow morning better?'
3. Confirm the exact time and the right number.
4. Set the agenda for the callback: 'When we talk at 6 I can have everything ready to go — is the plan to get this wrapped up then?'
5. Send a calendar confirmation or text if possible.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: This is not a great time. Can you call me back?
Agent: Absolutely. Would later today work or is tomorrow better for you?
Prospect: Tomorrow is better.
Agent: What time works — morning or afternoon?
Prospect: Around noon.
Agent: Perfect. I will call you at noon. And just so I am ready — when we talk tomorrow, is the plan to get this finalized?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Accepting 'call me later' without a specific time
- Not confirming the agenda for the callback
- Calling back and starting the pitch from scratch — they are already warm
- Being too aggressive about not getting off the phone — respect their time


PRACTICE SCENARIO

Early in the call, the prospect says they are busy right now and asks to be called back.

lessons.title: Not Interested
lessons.content:
They are not interested in your pitch. Find out what they are interested in.


WHY THIS WORKS

'Not interested' at the start of a call means they do not yet see the relevance to their life. It is a reflex, not a decision. The fastest way through this objection is to skip the pitch entirely and ask a single curious question that makes them feel heard instead of sold to. One good question can completely reset the dynamic.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Do not pitch past 'not interested' — stop immediately.
2. Acknowledge: 'I hear you. I am not going to pitch you on anything.'
3. Ask one question about their current situation — not about your product.
4. Listen. Let them talk.
5. If there is an opening — earn the right to present. If there is not — thank them and move on.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I'm really not interested.
Agent: Fair enough. I am not here to pitch you. Can I ask just one quick question — when is your home policy up for renewal?
Prospect: It renews in April I think.
Agent: Perfect timing actually. A lot of people we talk to in your area have been seeing rate increases at renewal this year. Would it be worth a quick five-minute comparison just so you know where you stand?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Pushing through 'not interested' with a pitch — guarantees a hang-up
- Asking too many questions after they said they are not interested
- Sounding scripted when they are already disengaged
- Not knowing when to let it go — some calls are genuinely not the right time


PRACTICE SCENARIO

First 30 seconds of an outbound call. The prospect says they are not interested before the agent has said much.

lessons.title: Already Have An Agent
lessons.content:
Having an agent is not the same as being well-served.


WHY THIS WORKS

The 'I already have an agent' objection is about loyalty and relationship, not about product. Address the relationship first. Your angle is not to attack their agent but to position yourself as a comparison resource. If their current agent has done a great job, you will confirm that and they will appreciate you for it. If there are gaps, the facts will speak for themselves.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Respect the relationship: 'That is great — having a dedicated agent is valuable.'
2. Reframe your call: 'I am not trying to replace them. I just want to make sure you have a fair comparison.'
3. Ask one question about their current experience.
4. Listen for any gap — service, price, response time, coverage.
5. If there is a gap, offer to address it. If there is not, acknowledge and thank them.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I already work with an agent I trust.
Agent: That is worth holding onto — a good agent relationship is hard to find. I am not here to replace them. I am just curious — when did they last proactively reach out to review your coverage?
Prospect: Honestly, not in a while.
Agent: That is the most common thing I hear. What if I just did a quick coverage check — not to take over your account, just to make sure you are not leaving anything on the table?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Attacking the current agent — creates defensiveness
- Pretending to be something you are not to get a foot in the door
- Not asking a follow-up question after they mention their agent
- Giving up immediately without exploring the relationship quality


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An outbound call where the prospect says they have a dedicated insurance agent they have worked with for years.

lessons.title: Bad Experience With Insurance
lessons.content:
Let them vent. Then separate yourself from whoever hurt them.


WHY THIS WORKS

A prospect with a bad insurance experience is not unsellable — they are actually highly motivated to find something better. But they need to feel heard before they can hear you. The formula is simple: let them tell the story, validate the frustration, separate yourself from the problem, and then make a new case. This is one of the few objections where more listening is the answer.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Invite them to share what happened: 'Can I ask what happened?'
2. Listen without interrupting or defending the industry.
3. Validate the frustration without throwing the previous carrier under the bus unnecessarily.
4. Separate yourself: 'That is exactly the kind of experience I work to prevent for my clients.'
5. Make a specific commitment about how you would handle their situation differently.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: Honestly I had a terrible experience with my last insurance company. They dropped me after a claim.
Agent: I am sorry to hear that. Can I ask what happened?
Prospect: I had a water damage claim and they raised my rates 40% and then did not renew me.
Agent: That is a nightmare situation and it happens more than it should with carriers who are not upfront about their claims tolerance. What I do for every client is explain exactly what the carrier's claims history policy is before we bind. No surprises. You deserve to know what you are signing up for.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Dismissing the experience: 'That is just how insurance works' — kills the relationship
- Defending the industry before you have built any trust
- Not making a specific commitment about how you would be different
- Rushing past the emotional part to get to the pitch


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An inbound call. The prospect is interested in quotes but immediately mentions they had a terrible experience with their last carrier.

lessons.title: Switching Feels Like A Hassle
lessons.content:
Make it effortless. The friction is in their head.


WHY THIS WORKS

The switching hassle objection is really a fear of the unknown process. Prospects imagine paperwork, gaps in coverage, having to cancel their old policy, and dealing with multiple companies. Your job is to walk them through exactly how simple the process actually is, eliminate each fear specifically, and make it clear that you handle the heavy lifting.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Acknowledge: 'Switching sounds complicated — but it really is not when it is done right.'
2. Walk through the exact steps and how simple each one is.
3. Be specific about what you handle versus what they have to do.
4. Address the cancellation of the old policy specifically.
5. Offer to walk them through it in real time while on the phone.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: Switching just seems like a lot of work.
Agent: I hear that a lot. Here is what actually happens: I get your new policy bound and active, you call your old carrier and cancel — that call takes about two minutes — and you are done. I will even tell you exactly what to say when you call them. The whole thing takes less time than you think. Want me to walk you through it?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Agreeing that it is complicated — validates the fear
- Being vague about the process — leaves the mystery intact
- Not specifically addressing the cancellation step which is usually the real fear
- Making the prospect do all the work instead of showing you handle it


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The prospect is interested in the quote and the price is better, but they say switching just feels like too much work.

lessons.title: Need To Check With My Bank / Mortgage Company
lessons.content:
This is a paperwork step, not a permission step.


WHY THIS WORKS

When a homeowner says they need to check with their mortgage company, they often believe they need permission to switch carriers. They do not. They have the right to choose any carrier that meets their mortgage company's minimum requirements. Your job is to clarify this misunderstanding, confirm that your carrier meets those requirements, and move forward.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Clarify the misunderstanding: 'You do not actually need their approval to switch — just notification.'
2. Confirm you meet their mortgage requirements: 'Our carrier is fully accepted by all major mortgage servicers.'
3. Explain the notification process — it is automatic in most cases.
4. Remove the objection entirely and re-close.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I think I need to check with my mortgage company before I switch.
Agent: You actually do not need their permission — you just need to notify them of the change, and that happens automatically when we bind the new policy. The mortgagee is added to the declarations page and they receive a copy directly. You do not have to do anything extra. Does that clear it up?
Prospect: Oh, I did not know that.
Agent: Most people do not. So there is nothing holding us up — let's get this locked in.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Telling them to go check with the bank and call back — unnecessary step
- Not explaining the automatic notification process
- Being vague about whether your carrier meets mortgage requirements
- Not re-closing immediately after clearing the objection


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A homeowner with a mortgage says they think they need approval from their lender before switching home insurance.

lessons.title: Let Me Google You First
lessons.content:
Welcome the research. You have nothing to hide.


WHY THIS WORKS

When a prospect says they want to look you or your company up before moving forward, that is a trust signal — they are doing due diligence, not rejecting you. The right response is to welcome the research and use it as an opportunity to direct them to the right information rather than leaving them to find the wrong thing.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Welcome it genuinely: 'Absolutely — that is a smart thing to do.'
2. Tell them exactly what to look for.
3. Give them the carrier's AM Best rating, BBB rating, or review sites.
4. Offer to stay on the line while they look, or schedule a specific callback.
5. If staying on the line — guide them to the right information.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: Let me look you guys up real quick before I commit to anything.
Agent: Please do — I encourage it. Look up the carrier on AM Best — we are rated A which is the top tier for financial stability. You can also check Google reviews. If you want, I can stay on the line while you pull it up so I can answer any questions in real time.
Prospect: Yeah, give me one second.
Agent: Take your time.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Getting defensive or trying to talk them out of looking
- Letting them go look and calling back later — you lose control of the timeline
- Not knowing what they will find when they do look
- Not offering to stay on the line during the search


PRACTICE SCENARIO

Near the close, the prospect says they want to look up the company online before making a decision.

lessons.title: Concern About Claim History
lessons.content:
A claim does not disqualify them. It changes the conversation.


WHY THIS WORKS

When a prospect reveals they have had recent claims, many agents tense up and start backpedaling. That is the wrong move. Claims are a fact of insurance. Your job is to find out the facts, be honest about how it affects their rate, and present the best available option given their profile. Honesty here builds trust that converts to long-term clients.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Ask about the claim factually — type, date, amount paid.
2. Do not overreact or get awkward — this is normal information.
3. Run the quote with the claim factored in.
4. Present the rate honestly and with context.
5. If the rate is high — reframe around the protection they are getting, not just the price.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I should tell you — I had a claim about two years ago.
Agent: Thanks for telling me. Can I ask — was it an at-fault auto claim, a home claim, or something else?
Prospect: It was a fender bender. My fault.
Agent: Got it. That will factor into the rate but with two years of clean history since then, you are actually in better shape than you think. Let me run the numbers and show you exactly where you land.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Reacting negatively to the claim information — makes them feel judged
- Overpromising that the claim will not affect the rate
- Not asking for the details of the claim before running the quote
- Abandoning the sale because of a claim without exploring all carrier options


PRACTICE SCENARIO

Mid-discovery, the prospect mentions they had an at-fault accident 18 months ago and is worried about being insurable.

lessons.title: Just Moved / Not Ready Yet
lessons.content:
The best time to get covered is before something goes wrong.


WHY THIS WORKS

A prospect who just moved is actually in an ideal buying moment — their old coverage may not apply to the new address, they have a life event creating natural urgency, and they are actively thinking about their home and assets. The 'just moved' objection is really a delay tactic from someone who has not connected the dots yet about why now is the exactly right time.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Validate the life event: 'Moving is a big deal — congratulations on the new place.'
2. Create immediate urgency: 'Did you know your old policy may not cover your new address?'
3. Educate on the coverage gap risk.
4. Offer to get them covered today — fast and simple.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: We just moved. I have not really had time to deal with insurance yet.
Agent: Congrats on the move. Quick question — did your old carrier transfer your coverage to the new address, or is that something you still need to set up?
Prospect: Honestly I am not sure.
Agent: That is worth finding out today because if it has not been updated, you may be in a coverage gap right now. Let me take five minutes and get you something solid so you are protected from day one in the new place.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Accepting 'I just moved, call me later' without addressing the coverage gap
- Not using the life event as genuine urgency
- Overwhelming a stressed new homeowner with too many options
- Not acknowledging the life event before jumping into the pitch


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A homeowner says they just moved into a new house two weeks ago and have not set up their insurance yet.

lessons.title: I'll Just Stay Month To Month
lessons.content:
Month-to-month costs them more. Show them the math.


WHY THIS WORKS

Prospects who want to stay month-to-month either do not understand that annual policies typically save money, or they are using it as a stall. Either way, the solution is simple math. Show them the actual dollar difference between month-to-month and annual, and make the decision a financial one rather than a commitment one.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Ask what is driving the month-to-month preference — flexibility or uncertainty.
2. If flexibility — explain that annual policies can usually be cancelled with a refund.
3. Show the annual savings in exact dollars.
4. Frame the annual commitment as the smarter financial choice.
5. Close on the annual option if possible; if not, close on monthly.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I would rather just go month to month for now.
Agent: Totally understand wanting flexibility. Here is something worth knowing — on a six-month or annual policy you would save about $220 compared to monthly. And most annual policies can be cancelled any time with a prorated refund. So you keep the flexibility but you are not paying extra for it. Does the annual make more sense when you look at it that way?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Not asking why they want month-to-month before responding
- Not showing the actual dollar savings
- Not mentioning the cancellation refund option which addresses the flexibility concern
- Accepting month-to-month without attempting the upgrade


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The prospect has agreed to move forward but says they prefer to pay month-to-month rather than committing to an annual policy.

lessons.title: My Rate Is Already Good
lessons.content:
Good compared to what? Make them prove it.


WHY THIS WORKS

A prospect who says their rate is already good usually has no frame of reference. They are comparing to their last renewal, not to the actual market. Your job is to create an honest comparison that either confirms their rate is competitive — which builds trust — or reveals a gap that creates a buying opportunity.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Validate: 'It might be — let's find out for sure.'
2. Ask for their current premium and basic coverage details.
3. Run a real comparison.
4. Present the result honestly: if they are getting a good deal, tell them. If not, show them the difference.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I think my rate is pretty competitive right now.
Agent: It might be. What are you paying currently?
Prospect: About $140 a month for home and auto.
Agent: And do you know your liability limits off the top of your head?
Prospect: 100/300 I think.
Agent: Let me run a real comparison on that profile. If you are at the right place, I will tell you and we can both move on. If not, I can save you money today. Fair enough?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Arguing that their rate is not good without running the numbers
- Not asking for their current rate details before comparing
- Being dishonest when the comparison is close — kills long-term trust
- Not closing if the comparison shows a real savings


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect called in but says they are probably not going to switch because their current rate is pretty good.

lessons.title: Bundling Resistance
lessons.content:
They do not want a bundle. They want a deal. Show them one.


WHY THIS WORKS

When prospects resist bundling, they usually either have a loyalty to their current auto carrier or they think keeping things separate gives them more control. The counter is simple: show them the bundle discount in real dollars, and show them that separate policies with two carriers actually creates gaps in coverage that a single bundled policy eliminates.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Ask why they prefer to keep them separate.
2. Address the specific reason — loyalty, complexity, or perception of control.
3. Show the bundle discount in exact dollar savings.
4. Explain the coverage coordination benefit of a single carrier.
5. Offer to run both scenarios side by side so they can see the difference.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I want to keep my auto where it is and just do home with you.
Agent: Totally fine. Can I show you one thing first? If we bundle both together here, the discount actually brings your total below what you are paying now for just home alone. Do you want me to run those numbers side by side so you can see the difference?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Pushing the bundle without understanding why they resist
- Not showing the actual dollar comparison
- Making the bundle feel like more complexity instead of more value
- Not offering to run both options — forcing instead of presenting


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The prospect wants a home quote but says they want to keep their auto policy where it currently is.

lessons.title: I Don't Own My Home / Just Renting
lessons.content:
Renters need coverage too. They just do not know it.


WHY THIS WORKS

Renters often believe their landlord's insurance covers their belongings. It does not. The landlord's policy covers the building. The renter's personal property, liability, and additional living expenses are completely unprotected without a renters policy. This is an education objection — once they understand the gap, the sale is simple.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Do not skip past this — it is a genuine education opportunity.
2. Explain what the landlord's policy does and does not cover.
3. Quantify their personal property exposure.
4. Present renters insurance as an obvious, inexpensive solution.
5. Close on the renters policy plus auto bundle for maximum savings.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I rent so I do not need home insurance.
Agent: That is actually a common misconception worth clearing up. Your landlord's insurance covers the building — not a single item that belongs to you. If there is a fire, your furniture, electronics, clothing — none of that is covered. A renters policy costs about $15 a month and protects everything inside. And when we bundle it with your auto, your auto rate drops too. Want me to run those numbers?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Skipping past the objection and only trying to sell auto
- Not explaining what the landlord's policy actually covers
- Quoting renters insurance without the bundle opportunity
- Being preachy about why they should have renters insurance


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An auto lead says they rent and therefore do not think they need home insurance.

lessons.title: Credit Score Concern
lessons.content:
Credit affects rate but never disqualifies. Be honest and find the best fit.


WHY THIS WORKS

Many prospects are afraid to get a quote because they assume bad credit means they cannot get insurance or will be charged unaffordable rates. The reality is that while credit does affect insurance scores, there are carriers who are more lenient on credit than others — and no one is completely uninsurable. Your job is to remove the fear, run the quote honestly, and present the best available option for their profile.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Remove the fear upfront: 'Credit is one factor but it does not disqualify you.'
2. Explain briefly how insurance credit scoring works.
3. Run the quote — do not pre-apologize for the rate before you know it.
4. Present the result honestly and recommend the best carrier for their profile.
5. If the rate is high due to credit, explain what improves over time.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I should warn you — my credit is not great.
Agent: I appreciate you telling me. Credit is one of the factors carriers use but it does not stop you from getting covered. Some carriers weigh it more than others — my job is to find which one gives you the best rate for your specific profile. Let me run it and I will show you exactly what comes back.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Pre-apologizing for the rate before seeing it
- Overexplaining credit scoring in a way that sounds like a lecture
- Not knowing which carriers are most lenient on credit
- Avoiding the subject and letting the prospect discover the high rate without context


PRACTICE SCENARIO

Early in a call, the prospect warns the agent that they have poor credit and are worried it will affect their insurability.

courses.title: Discovery & Needs Analysis
courses.description: 12 drills on uncovering coverage gaps, prior claims, budget, decision makers, and real urgency before ever presenting a quote.

lessons.title: Opening Discovery Questions
lessons.content:
The first three questions set the entire tone of the call.


WHY THIS WORKS

The opening discovery questions are not information-gathering exercises — they are relationship-building tools. The right opening questions signal to the prospect that you are different from every other agent who called them. They show that you are curious about their situation, not just trying to run a quote. The best opening discovery questions are open-ended, specific to their situation, and give the prospect a chance to talk about themselves.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Start with context: 'Before I run any numbers, I want to make sure I understand your situation.'
2. Ask about their current coverage first — not what they want, but what they have.
3. Ask about their history with their carrier — how long, any claims, any issues.
4. Ask about what prompted the call or the comparison.
5. Listen more than you talk. Discovery is not a monologue.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Before I pull anything up — can I ask how long you have been with your current carrier?
Prospect: About five years.
Agent: And in those five years have they proactively reviewed your coverage, or has it just renewed automatically?
Prospect: Mostly just renewed on its own.
Agent: That is the most common story I hear. What made you decide to take a look now?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Going straight to the quote without any discovery
- Asking closed yes/no questions that give you no usable information
- Interrupting the prospect before they finish their answer
- Not using the discovery information later in the recommendation


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent just answered an inbound call from a prospect who wants a home and auto quote. The agent needs to run quality discovery before quoting.

lessons.title: Uncovering Coverage Gaps
lessons.content:
Most people are underinsured and do not know it.


WHY THIS WORKS

Coverage gaps are the most valuable discovery you can do for a prospect. When you find a real gap — inadequate liability, wrong dwelling coverage, missing umbrella, no loss-of-use protection — you have just created genuine value. The prospect was not aware of the problem until you found it. That is the difference between an agent and an advisor. This drill trains you to systematically look for gaps in every call.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Ask for the prospect's declarations page or at minimum their current coverage limits.
2. Review liability limits — most people have state minimum which is dangerously low.
3. Check dwelling coverage — often set too low due to inflation or renovations.
4. Ask about umbrella policy — most homeowners with significant assets have no umbrella.
5. Ask about loss of use coverage — what happens if they can't live in their home during a claim.
6. Present each gap as a discovery, not as a sales pitch.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Can you tell me what your liability limit is on your auto policy right now?
Prospect: I think it is 50/100.
Agent: That is actually below what most financial advisors recommend for a homeowner. If you are at fault in an accident and the medical bills exceed $50,000, the rest comes from your personal assets — your home equity included. Has anyone ever walked you through that risk before?
Prospect: No, honestly.
Agent: That is the conversation I want to make sure we have today.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Not asking for current coverage details before quoting
- Presenting coverage gaps as sales tactics instead of genuine concerns
- Overwhelming the prospect with every possible gap at once
- Not connecting the gap to their specific assets and life situation


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect has been with the same carrier for 7 years and has never had a coverage review. The agent suspects they are underinsured.

lessons.title: Life Event Discovery
lessons.content:
Life changes create coverage needs. Find them.


WHY THIS WORKS

Life events — marriage, new baby, home purchase, teenager getting a license, retirement, home renovation — each create new insurance needs or change existing ones. Agents who discover these events create enormous value and build long-term client relationships. This drill trains you to listen for life events and connect them directly to coverage decisions.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Ask about recent changes: 'Has anything changed in your household in the last year or two?'
2. Listen for: new drivers, home improvements, major purchases, family size changes.
3. Connect each life event to a specific coverage implication.
4. Present the solution as a response to their life, not as a product pitch.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Has anything changed at home in the last year or so — any renovations, new family members, new cars?
Prospect: Yeah, my son just turned 16 and started driving.
Agent: Congratulations and condolences at the same time. Adding a teenage driver is one of the biggest rate events in auto insurance — and how it is handled varies a lot by carrier. Let me make sure you are with the right one for your household profile now.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Not asking about life events at all — leaves the biggest needs undiscovered
- Asking too many questions about changes without connecting them to solutions
- Not listening for life events that the prospect mentions casually in passing
- Missing the opportunity to build a long-term multi-policy relationship


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A renewal quote call with an existing policyholder. The agent needs to discover any life changes before making recommendations.

lessons.title: Budget Discovery Without Killing Value
lessons.content:
Ask about budget without making price the anchor.


WHY THIS WORKS

Asking about budget is necessary but dangerous if done wrong. If you ask 'What's your budget?' too early, you have anchored the conversation to price before you have built any value. The right way to discover budget is late in discovery, after you have established what good coverage looks like for them, and framed it around what they are currently paying — not what they want to pay.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Build value through coverage discovery before touching price.
2. Ask what they are currently paying — not what they want to pay.
3. Find out if they have shopped before and what rates they have seen.
4. Use their current payment as the comparison benchmark, not a budget ceiling.
5. Never lead with price — lead with what the right coverage looks like.


EXAMPLE

Agent: So based on what we have talked about — the liability limits, the dwelling coverage, keeping both cars on the same policy — what are you paying right now combined?
Prospect: About $280 a month for both.
Agent: Okay. And is the goal to improve coverage, reduce the rate, or both?
Prospect: Both if possible, but coverage is the priority.
Agent: That is exactly the right answer. Let me show you what we can do.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Asking 'What's your budget?' at the start of the call
- Using the budget as a ceiling that caps what you present
- Not asking what they are currently paying before quoting
- Making price the primary focus instead of coverage and value


PRACTICE SCENARIO

Mid-discovery on a home and auto bundle call. The agent needs to understand the financial picture without letting price dominate the conversation.

lessons.title: Household Decision Maker Discovery
lessons.content:
Selling to the wrong person wastes both of your time.


WHY THIS WORKS

Before you invest 20 minutes building a relationship and presenting a quote, you need to know if you are talking to the person who can say yes. This is not about being rude — it is about being efficient. The way you discover decision-making authority without offending anyone is through casual, natural questions about the household that reveal who else is in the picture.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Early in discovery, ask casually about the household: 'Is it just yourself on the policy or do we need to include a spouse or partner?'
2. If there is a partner, ask if they are involved in this kind of decision.
3. If yes — attempt to get them on the call or schedule when both are available.
4. Do not present a full close to someone who cannot say yes.
5. Build a strong recommendation that they can present to the decision maker if needed.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Is the policy just in your name or do you have a spouse or partner we need to include?
Prospect: My husband is on everything too.
Agent: Got it. Is he someone who is involved in decisions like this or do you handle the insurance?
Prospect: We usually decide together on bigger stuff.
Agent: Perfect. Is he available to jump on real quick? I can walk you both through it in about 10 minutes so you are on the same page when we get to the numbers.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Not asking about the decision maker until after the full pitch
- Assuming the person on the phone is the sole decision maker
- Not attempting to get the other decision maker on the call
- Getting frustrated when a spouse objection comes at the close because it was not discovered earlier


PRACTICE SCENARIO

Early in an inbound home and auto quote call. The agent needs to establish who the decision makers are before investing time in a full presentation.

lessons.title: Pain Point Extraction
lessons.content:
People buy to solve problems. Find the problem first.


WHY THIS WORKS

Pain points are the emotional engine of every sale. A prospect buys when they connect your solution to a real problem they have. Surface-level discovery finds coverage needs. Deep discovery finds the fear, frustration, or past experience that makes someone actually want to change. This drill trains you to go deeper than the standard quote questions.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. After learning the basics, go deeper: 'What is the main thing you are hoping to fix or improve?'
2. Ask about past experiences: 'Have you ever had a claim? How was it handled?'
3. Ask about fears: 'What is your biggest concern when it comes to your coverage?'
4. Listen for emotional language — frustration, anxiety, regret.
5. Use their pain point language in your recommendation.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Let me ask you something — if you could change one thing about your current coverage or experience with your carrier, what would it be?
Prospect: Honestly, I just want to know someone is going to answer the phone if I ever need to file a claim. My last company was impossible to reach.
Agent: That is the most important thing and most people do not find out until it is too late. Service quality at claim time is something I specifically help people evaluate. Let me tell you what to look for.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Only asking fact-based questions and missing the emotional layer
- Not using the pain point in the recommendation
- Rushing past pain points to get to the pitch
- Minimizing the prospect's frustration before building your solution


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect who has been shopping for insurance for a few weeks. The agent needs to understand why they are shopping and what has not worked about their current situation.

lessons.title: Prior Claims Discovery
lessons.content:
Know before you quote. Claims change everything.


WHY THIS WORKS

Discovering prior claims early in the call is one of the most important things you can do — for your credibility and for the prospect's experience. Nothing destroys trust faster than presenting a rate and then having it change because of a claim that was not disclosed upfront. This drill trains you to ask about claims naturally, early, and without making the prospect feel like they are being interrogated.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Ask about claims as part of your natural discovery flow, not as a checklist item.
2. Frame it as something that helps you find the right carrier for their profile.
3. Ask specifically: auto claims, home claims, and how recent.
4. Adjust your carrier recommendations based on claim history.
5. Be honest about how claims affect rate — do not pretend they do not.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Before I run this through the system — I want to make sure I find the right carrier for your profile. Have you had any auto or home claims in the last five years?
Prospect: I had a windshield claim on the auto about two years ago.
Agent: Good to know. Comprehensive claims like windshield are treated differently than at-fault accidents — most carriers do not penalize much for those. I will make sure we go with one that is friendly on that profile.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Not asking about claims until the quote comes back high
- Making the prospect feel judged for having claims
- Not knowing which carriers are most lenient on specific claim types
- Presenting a rate that will change at binding because of undiscovered claims


PRACTICE SCENARIO

Early discovery on an auto quote. The agent needs to ask about claims in a natural, non-judgmental way.

lessons.title: Urgency Discovery
lessons.content:
Every call has urgency. Find it before you close.


WHY THIS WORKS

Urgency makes the close easier. Most agents invent urgency at the end of a call because they did not discover real urgency during it. This drill trains you to listen for and develop real urgency throughout discovery — renewal dates, lapse risks, life changes, rate increases at renewal — so that when you close, the urgency is already established and the timing makes obvious sense.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Ask about renewal dates early: 'When does your current policy renew?'
2. Ask about rate changes: 'Did your rate change at your last renewal?'
3. Listen for life events that create coverage urgency.
4. Note the urgency points and return to them at the close.
5. Never manufacture urgency — use only what you discover.


EXAMPLE

Agent: When does your current policy renew?
Prospect: I think it is coming up in about three weeks.
Agent: That is actually good timing. If you are making a change, doing it before the renewal means you avoid paying for another term you do not need. Let's make sure we get something in place before that date.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Not asking about renewal dates until the close
- Inventing urgency with fake deadlines
- Discovering urgency and not using it — leaving a powerful closing tool on the table
- Making urgency feel like pressure instead of practical timing


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A mid-call moment where the agent has completed basic discovery and is transitioning toward the presentation.

lessons.title: Multi-Policy Discovery
lessons.content:
Every single-line client is a multi-line opportunity waiting to happen.


WHY THIS WORKS

Multi-policy discovery is about building a complete picture of every insurance need the household has — not just the one they called about. An agent who only quotes what the prospect asks for is an order taker. An agent who discovers and addresses all their needs is an advisor. This drill trains you to systematically identify every policy opportunity in a household.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. After establishing the primary need, ask about adjacent policies.
2. If auto — ask about home, renters, life, umbrella.
3. If home — ask about auto, jewelry, watercraft, life.
4. Frame the discovery as looking out for their complete protection, not trying to sell more.
5. Present bundle savings as a benefit, not a sales tactic.


EXAMPLE

Agent: You mentioned you have two cars. Do you also own your home or are you renting?
Prospect: We own.
Agent: And is your home policy with the same carrier as your auto right now?
Prospect: No, they are separate.
