Agent: That is actually the most common setup and it is usually the most expensive one. When we bundle them together, the discount on both policies is usually enough to make it worth moving everything. Want me to run the bundle number so you can see the difference?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Only quoting the line they called about and missing the broader household
- Pitching the bundle before establishing the need for it
- Not asking about home when the primary call is auto, and vice versa
- Making multi-policy discovery feel like upselling instead of advising


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An inbound auto quote call. The agent has completed auto discovery and needs to naturally expand into the broader household insurance picture.

lessons.title: Liability Exposure Questions
lessons.content:
Most people have no idea how exposed they are.


WHY THIS WORKS

Liability is the most underserved coverage in personal insurance. Most people carry the minimum because they were never educated on what it actually means to be underinsured for liability. This discovery drill trains you to surface the real liability risk in a household — assets, net worth, high-traffic home situations, teenage drivers — and connect it directly to a coverage solution.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Ask about household profile: own a home, net worth, equity, assets.
2. Ask about teenage drivers or high-risk situations.
3. Educate: 'If you are sued for more than your liability limit, they can come after your personal assets.'
4. Recommend appropriate limits based on their profile.
5. Introduce umbrella policy if the household has significant assets.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Do you have a rough sense of your home equity right now?
Prospect: Maybe $150,000 in equity at this point.
Agent: That is significant. Your liability coverage is what protects that if you are at fault in an accident and someone sues you. Right now on state minimum liability, if medical bills exceed $25,000 the difference comes from your assets — including that equity. Does anyone ever talk to you about that?
Prospect: No, never.
Agent: That is the most important conversation I can have with a homeowner. Let's fix that today.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Not asking about assets before recommending liability limits
- Recommending the same liability limits to everyone regardless of their exposure
- Not explaining umbrella coverage to high-asset households
- Making liability risk sound like fear-mongering instead of practical planning


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A homeowner with good credit and significant equity is shopping for home and auto. The agent needs to surface their real liability exposure.

lessons.title: Current Policy Deep Dive
lessons.content:
You cannot improve what you do not understand.


WHY THIS WORKS

A current policy deep dive means getting the full picture of what a prospect currently has before you quote them on something new. Most agents skip this and end up either quoting apples to oranges or missing obvious improvement opportunities. When you know exactly what they have, you can show them exactly what they are missing — and that is the most powerful sales conversation you can have.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Ask for their declarations page or key coverage details.
2. Go line by line: liability limits, deductibles, coverage types, endorsements.
3. Note what they have, what they are missing, and what is excessive.
4. Build your recommendation around improving specifically on what they told you.
5. Reference their current policy details throughout your presentation — it shows you were listening.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Before I run any quotes, I want to make sure I understand exactly what you have right now. Do you have your declarations page handy or can you pull it up on your phone?
Prospect: Yeah, I can pull it up.
Agent: Perfect. Let's go through it together. I want to see your liability limits, your deductible, and whether you have replacement cost or actual cash value on your personal property.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Quoting without knowing what they currently have
- Only asking about premium and not about coverage details
- Not using their current policy information in the recommendation
- Making them feel like the current policy review is just a sales setup


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An inbound shopping call where the prospect currently has coverage but is considering switching. The agent needs to understand the current policy before recommending a replacement.

lessons.title: Future Needs Discovery
lessons.content:
The best clients are the ones you grow with.


WHY THIS WORKS

Future needs discovery is how you build a long-term client relationship from a single transaction. By asking about what is coming in the next one to two years — home purchase, new car, getting married, starting a business — you position yourself as the advisor they come back to when those events happen. This is relationship-building disguised as discovery.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. After completing current needs discovery, ask about the near future.
2. Ask: 'Any big changes coming up in the next year or two? New car, moving, family changes?'
3. Note everything relevant.
4. Mention how those future events will affect their coverage.
5. Plant the seed for the future relationship: 'When that happens, make sure you call me before you do anything.'


EXAMPLE

Agent: Looking ahead — any big changes coming up? New car, planning to buy a home, anything like that?
Prospect: Actually yeah, we are looking at buying a house in the next six months.
Agent: That is a big one. When you are ready to close, home insurance needs to be in place before the closing date. Call me about two weeks before — I will have everything ready so that piece is one less thing you have to worry about.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Not asking about the future at all — misses relationship-building opportunities
- Asking about the future and then forgetting to follow up when the event happens
- Not making a specific commitment to be their resource for the future event
- Making the future needs question feel like a sales fishing expedition


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An auto-only quote call. The agent has completed the sale and is building the long-term relationship before getting off the phone.

courses.title: Opening & Rapport
courses.description: 10 drills on the first 10 seconds of a call, warm transfers, building genuine rapport, and setting an agenda that earns the rest of the conversation.

lessons.title: First 10 Seconds
lessons.content:
The call is won or lost before you say your name.


WHY THIS WORKS

The first ten seconds of any call set the prospect's entire mental frame for the conversation. They are making a split-second judgment: is this a real professional who can help me, or is this another telemarketer I need to get off the phone? Your opening must convey authority, purpose, and warmth simultaneously. There is no time to warm up — you are either compelling from the first word or you are fighting for attention the entire call.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Answer or open with full energy — not flat, not hyper, just present and confident.
2. State your name and company clearly.
3. State the purpose of the call in one sentence that is about them, not about you.
4. Give them a reason to stay engaged in the first 15 words.
5. Do not read from a script — it sounds like a script.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Hey, this is Marcus with Premier Insurance. I am following up on the quote request you submitted — looks like you are shopping home and auto. I have a couple of questions before I pull numbers so I can make sure what I show you actually makes sense for your situation.
Prospect: Oh yeah, I did fill that out. Sure, go ahead.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Opening with 'Hi, how are you today?' — sounds like every telemarketer
- Stating your company before your name — puts them in defensive mode
- Being too formal or too casual — neither matches the tone of a trusted advisor
- Not stating the purpose of the call immediately — leaves them wondering why you called


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent is making an outbound call to a lead who submitted a home and auto quote request online 20 minutes ago.

lessons.title: Warm Transfer Takeover
lessons.content:
You have 30 seconds to own the call before they check out.


WHY THIS WORKS

When a prospect is transferred to you, they have already been on the phone with someone else and their patience may be thin. The warm transfer takeover drill trains you to immediately establish credibility, acknowledge the transfer smoothly, and transition into your own discovery without missing a beat. The prospect needs to feel like they landed with the right person.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Greet them using their first name — it should have been given to you in the transfer.
2. Acknowledge the transfer briefly: 'I have your information here.'
3. Immediately establish your role and what you are about to do for them.
4. Ask one warm-up question before going into discovery.
5. Do not start from scratch — build on whatever rapport the transferring agent established.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Hey Sarah, this is James — I am the licensed advisor here and I have your information pulled up. I understand you are looking at home and auto today. Before I run any numbers — real quick, is it just the two of you in the household or do you have other drivers we need to include?
Prospect: It is me, my husband, and our daughter — she just got her license.
Agent: Got it. That is actually really helpful to know upfront because that changes which carrier is going to give you the best rate. Let me ask you a few more things.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Starting completely from scratch as if the prospect has not already been on a call
- Not using their name immediately
- Sounding uncertain about why they were transferred to you
- Going straight to the quote without any personal connection


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent just received a warm transfer from a call center. The prospect's name is Sarah and she requested a home and auto quote.

lessons.title: Name Usage Throughout The Call
lessons.content:
The sweetest sound to anyone is their own name.


WHY THIS WORKS

Using a prospect's name throughout a call builds connection and personalizes what could otherwise feel like a transactional interaction. But there is an art to it — use it too much and it sounds manipulative. Use it too little and the call feels generic. This drill trains you on the right frequency, the right moments, and the right tone for name usage on an insurance sales call.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Get the name right at the start — confirm the pronunciation if it is unfamiliar.
2. Use their name at key transition moments: when making a recommendation, when asking for the sale, when addressing an objection.
3. Use it naturally in conversation — not as a sentence opener every time.
4. Never use it in a way that sounds scripted: 'So Bob, what I want to tell you Bob is...'
5. Aim for 3 to 5 natural uses per call.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Based on everything you told me, Jennifer — this policy covers exactly what you were looking for and comes in under your current rate.
Agent: Does this feel like the right move for your household, Jennifer?
Prospect: Yeah, I think so.
Agent: Let's get it locked in.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Never using their name — the call feels impersonal
- Using it too frequently — sounds robotic and manipulative
- Using it as a filler: 'Well John, that's a great question John...'
- Mispronouncing the name after being corrected


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A full mock call where the agent practices natural, well-timed name usage throughout all stages — opening, discovery, recommendation, and close.

lessons.title: Cold To Warm Opener
lessons.content:
Turn a stranger into a conversation in 60 seconds.


WHY THIS WORKS

A cold call opener is different from an inbound opener because the prospect was not expecting you and has no inherent interest. The goal in the first 60 seconds is not to sell — it is to earn the right to have a conversation. You do that by leading with relevance to their situation, not with your product or company.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Open with something specific to them — their address, their renewal window, something they would recognize.
2. Give them one compelling reason to stay on the phone in the first sentence.
3. Ask a question immediately — it shifts them from passive to active.
4. Keep the opener under 20 seconds before you get them talking.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Hi, is this Michael? Great — I am calling because I noticed your home in the 30004 zip code may be significantly overcharged for home insurance based on current market rates. I am not going to pitch you anything — I just want to ask you one question. When did you last actually compare your home rate?
Prospect: Probably three years ago honestly.
Agent: That is actually a significant amount of time in this market. A lot has changed with rates. Would you be open to a five-minute comparison?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Starting with a long company introduction
- Asking 'Did I catch you at a bad time?' — gives them an easy out
- Not getting them talking within the first 30 seconds
- Pitching the product before earning permission to have the conversation


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An outbound cold call to a homeowner in a target zip code who has not requested a quote.

lessons.title: Finding Common Ground
lessons.content:
People buy from people they like. Give them a reason to like you.


WHY THIS WORKS

Common ground is not small talk for its own sake — it is the bridge between stranger and trusted advisor. When you find something genuine to connect on — shared location, shared experience, shared concern — the entire dynamic of the call shifts. You become a person, not a salesperson. This drill trains you to find common ground quickly and use it to build the kind of rapport that keeps prospects on the phone.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Listen during the first few exchanges for any personal detail you can connect on.
2. When you find something, engage with it genuinely — not as a technique.
3. Keep it brief — two to three exchanges maximum before getting back to business.
4. Refer back to it naturally later in the call if it is relevant.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: We just moved here from Ohio actually.
Agent: Ohio — what part?
Prospect: Columbus area.
Agent: I have family in Columbus. The winters here must feel like a vacation. Have you adjusted to the weather?
Prospect: Oh completely — I am never going back.
Agent: Ha — one thing worth knowing about weather here though is that storm coverage is different than what you might be used to. Let me make sure we have you set up right for this area.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Forcing common ground that is not there
- Spending too long on small talk before getting to business
- Using common ground as a manipulation tool instead of a genuine connection
- Not connecting the rapport back to a relevant business point


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An inbound call where the prospect mentions they recently moved to the area. The agent needs to build genuine rapport while staying on purpose.

lessons.title: Setting The Call Agenda
lessons.content:
Tell them where you are going. They will follow.


WHY THIS WORKS

Setting the agenda at the start of a call does two things: it establishes you as the professional in control of the conversation, and it reduces the prospect's anxiety about where the call is going. When people know what to expect, they relax. When they relax, they engage. A good agenda-setting statement takes 15 seconds and completely changes the tone of everything that follows.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. After your opening, briefly describe what the call will look like.
2. Give it a time frame: 'This will take about 10 to 15 minutes.'
3. Tell them what you will cover: discovery, quote, options.
4. Tell them what happens at the end — they decide, no pressure.
5. Get their buy-in: 'Does that work for you?'


EXAMPLE

Agent: Here is how I want to run this. I am going to ask you about 5 to 6 questions about your current coverage and situation — that takes about 5 minutes. Then I will run the numbers and show you exactly what the best option looks like for your household. At the end, you decide if it makes sense. Total time is about 15 minutes. Does that work?
Prospect: Yeah that's fine.
Agent: Perfect. Let's start with — how long have you been with your current carrier?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Not setting an agenda at all — prospect does not know what they signed up for
- Setting an agenda that sounds like a sales script
- Giving a time estimate and then going over it significantly
- Not getting their buy-in before starting the call


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The opening of an inbound quote call. The prospect has agreed to hear about options. The agent needs to set the agenda before starting discovery.

lessons.title: Earned Authority Opener
lessons.content:
Establish expertise early. It makes everything else land harder.


WHY THIS WORKS

Earned authority means giving the prospect a specific, credible reason to trust your expertise before you say anything else. It is not bragging — it is context. When you say 'I specialize in households with teenage drivers' or 'I work primarily with homeowners in this zip code,' you become the right expert for their situation before you have asked a single question. This changes how they listen to everything that follows.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Identify the prospect's specific situation from the lead data.
2. Craft a one-sentence authority statement that is specific to their situation.
3. Deliver it naturally — not as a credential list.
4. Immediately transition to a question about their specific situation.


EXAMPLE

Agent: I specialize specifically in home and auto for homeowners in this area and I have put together a lot of bundles for families with profiles like yours. Before I run anything, I want to make sure I ask the right questions so what I show you actually fits. Sound good?
Prospect: Sure, go for it.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Listing credentials instead of making them relevant to the prospect
- Sounding like you are reading an 'about me' page
- Not transitioning immediately to a question after establishing authority
- Overclaiming expertise you do not actually have


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An outbound call to a lead who requested an auto quote and mentioned having a teenage driver. The agent needs to establish relevant expertise immediately.

lessons.title: Referral Opener
lessons.content:
A name is a shortcut to trust.


WHY THIS WORKS

A referral call is the highest-conversion opportunity in insurance sales. Someone who already trusts you has vouched for you before you even said hello. The referral opener maximizes that head start by leading with the name immediately, acknowledging the relationship warmly, and transitioning to discovery without wasting the trust equity you have been given.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Lead with the referrer's name in the first sentence.
2. Acknowledge the relationship warmly — not transactionally.
3. Explain briefly how you helped the referrer.
4. Pivot to their specific situation.
5. Do not assume they know anything about you — earn it.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Hi, is this Dave? Hey Dave — your neighbor Tom Williams suggested I reach out. I helped Tom put together a home and auto bundle earlier this year and he saved about $600 annually. He thought I might be able to do something similar for you. Is now an okay time to take a look at your situation?
Prospect: Oh yeah, Tom mentioned you. Sure, what do you need?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Mentioning the referrer's name without connecting it to a specific outcome
- Being too casual about the referral as if it is an assumed connection
- Not asking for permission to continue before launching into the pitch
- Overclaiming what you did for the referrer


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A call to a referral from an existing client. The prospect's name is Dave and the referrer is a neighbor named Tom.

lessons.title: Reactivation Opener
lessons.content:
Dead leads are not dead. They are just waiting for the right reason.


WHY THIS WORKS

A reactivation call is to a prospect who previously showed interest but did not buy. They went cold for a reason — usually timing, not disinterest. The reactivation opener acknowledges the history, gives them a new reason to engage, and does not restart from scratch. Treating a reactivation like a cold call is the number one mistake agents make with old leads.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Reference the previous contact briefly and without apology.
2. Give them a new, specific reason why reaching out now makes sense.
3. Do not pitch — ask one question about whether their situation has changed.
4. If the timing is still wrong, lock in a follow-up before getting off the phone.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Hey Lisa, this is Jason — we spoke about three months ago about your home and auto and the timing was not right. I wanted to reach out because rates in your area have actually come down recently and I thought it was worth taking another look. Has anything changed on your end since we talked?
Prospect: Actually yeah — we just refinanced so we are looking at our whole financial picture again.
Agent: Perfect timing. Let's see what we can do.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Pretending the previous call never happened — loses credibility
- Apologizing for calling again — signals weakness
- Not giving them a new reason to engage — same pitch, same result
- Not asking if anything has changed — assumes the same situation


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An outbound call to a lead from 90 days ago who got a quote but did not buy. The agent is calling back with a new rate update.

lessons.title: Mirroring Tone
lessons.content:
Match their energy. Lead them somewhere better.


WHY THIS WORKS

Tone mirroring is the unconscious rapport-building technique that the best salespeople use without thinking. If the prospect is rushed, they need brevity. If they are chatty, they want conversation. If they are skeptical, they need facts. The mistake agents make is bringing a fixed tone to every call instead of reading and matching the prospect's energy. This drill trains you to quickly read tone and adjust before the prospect tunes you out.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. In the first 30 seconds, identify the prospect's pace, energy, and mood.
2. Match their pace — fast-talker gets a faster opener, slow deliberate talker gets measured conversation.
3. Match their formality level — some people want professionalism, others want human.
4. Lead them gradually to a more engaged, open state.
5. Do not mirror negativity or frustration — mirror the energy underneath it.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: Yeah, hi, I don't have a lot of time.
Agent: I will be quick. Two questions, 90 seconds, and I will tell you if I can save you money on home and auto. Fair?
Prospect: Fine, go.
Agent: How long have you been with your current carrier and have your rates gone up in the last year?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Bringing high energy to a quiet, skeptical prospect — creates friction
- Slowing down for a rushed prospect instead of being more direct
- Matching frustration or negativity — amplifies the bad energy
- Not adjusting after the first 30 seconds when you have better information


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect answers the phone quickly and signals they are busy and have limited time. The agent needs to match that energy immediately.

courses.title: Follow-Up & Pipeline
courses.description: 10 drills for staying on a lead — same-day follow-up, voicemail and text scripts, reviving dead leads, and keeping a pipeline under control instead of letting it go cold.

lessons.title: Same-Day Follow-Up Call
lessons.content:
The fastest follow-up wins. Always.


WHY THIS WORKS

Same-day follow-up is the most powerful sales move in your pipeline. When someone requests a quote, talks to you for 20 minutes, and does not buy, their interest is highest in the hours immediately after. The longer you wait, the more their life takes over and the more competitors get in front of them. This drill trains you to make a compelling same-day follow-up call that re-engages without feeling desperate.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Call within 2 to 3 hours of the original conversation.
2. Reference something specific from your conversation — not generic.
3. Give them a new angle, new information, or a specific answer to a question they had.
4. Move directly to re-closing — do not start the pitch from scratch.
5. If they do not answer, leave a voicemail that makes them want to call back.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Hey Mark — it's Jason. We talked this afternoon about your home and auto. I thought of something after our call — you mentioned your roof was replaced two years ago. I ran it through one more carrier that actually rewards recent roof replacement and the rate came back $40 lower than what I showed you. Can you talk for 5 minutes?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Waiting until the next day to follow up
- Calling back with nothing new — 'Just checking in' is not a reason to call
- Not referencing the specific conversation — sounds like a cold call
- Being apologetic or timid in the follow-up tone


PRACTICE SCENARIO

It is 3 hours after a call where the prospect said they needed to think about it. The agent is calling back with a new piece of information.

lessons.title: Voicemail That Gets Called Back
lessons.content:
Most voicemails are never returned. Yours will be.


WHY THIS WORKS

The average insurance voicemail says 'Hi, this is [name] from [company], call me back at [number].' Nobody calls back. A voicemail that gets returned has two things: a specific reason to call back and a deadline. This drill trains you to leave concise, compelling voicemails that create curiosity and urgency without being gimmicky.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Keep it under 25 seconds.
2. State your name and that you spoke before OR that you have specific information.
3. Give them one specific reason to call back — a number, a rate, an answer.
4. Give a soft deadline if you have one.
5. End with your number said slowly and clearly, twice.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Hey Lisa, this is Marcus with Premier Insurance. We spoke last week about your home rate. I have an updated quote that came back better than what I showed you — $30 lower per month. I want to make sure you see this before the rate lock expires Friday. Give me a call back at 770-555-0194. Again, 770-555-0194. Thanks Lisa.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Leaving a voicemail with no specific reason to call back
- Going over 30 seconds — they stop listening
- Not saying your phone number twice
- Sounding like you are reading from a script


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent is calling a prospect who got a quote three days ago and has not responded to two emails. This is a practice drill for leaving compelling voicemails.

lessons.title: Text Follow-Up Script
lessons.content:
Texts get read. Make yours worth reading.


WHY THIS WORKS

Text messages have a 98% open rate compared to 20% for email. A well-crafted follow-up text can re-engage a prospect who has gone quiet. But most sales texts are either too salesy or too vague. This drill trains you to write short, conversational, specific texts that feel like they came from a person — not a mass campaign.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Keep the text under 3 sentences.
2. Reference something specific from your conversation.
3. Ask one direct question or give one specific piece of information.
4. Do not send a wall of text — it will not be read.
5. End with a question that is easy to answer.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Hey Mark, it's Jason from Premier. Ran your profile through one more carrier — came back $35 lower. Worth 5 minutes?
Prospect: Yeah send me the details
Agent: Calling you now.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Sending a multi-paragraph text — it gets ignored
- Not personalizing the text to their specific situation
- Sending texts at bad times — early morning, late evening
- Not following up a positive text response immediately with a call


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect from two days ago who has not responded to a voicemail. The agent is crafting and sending a follow-up text.

lessons.title: Email Follow-Up
lessons.content:
A good follow-up email is short, specific, and impossible to ignore.


WHY THIS WORKS

A follow-up email is not a quote dump or a product brochure. It is a short, personal message with a specific call to action. The best follow-up emails look like they were written in two minutes by someone who was thinking about the prospect — because they were. This drill trains you to write emails that actually get responded to.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Subject line: specific, not generic. 'Re: Your home + auto quote' beats 'Following Up'
2. First line: reference the specific conversation.
3. Middle: one piece of value — the quote, the savings amount, the answer to their question.
4. End: one clear call to action.
5. No attachments unless they specifically asked for them.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Subject: Your home + auto bundle — $47/mo savings

Hi Lisa,

Following up from our call Tuesday. I ran the bundle through three carriers and Travelers came back the strongest for your profile — $47 a month less than what you are paying now with better liability limits.

When can we get on the phone for 10 minutes to get this finalized?

Jason


COMMON MISTAKES

- Writing long emails that require a reading commitment to get to the point
- Attaching a quote document instead of just giving the number
- Using a generic subject line that gets buried in their inbox
- Not having a specific call to action — 'Let me know if you have questions' is not an action


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect from a call earlier in the week. They asked to receive something by email. The agent needs to write a follow-up email that re-engages them.

lessons.title: Dead Lead Resurrection
lessons.content:
Your best leads are the ones you already built rapport with.


WHY THIS WORKS

A dead lead is not a closed door — it is a conversation that stopped at the wrong moment. People's situations change. Rates change. Life changes. A lead you worked three months ago and lost may be ready to buy today for a completely different reason. This drill trains you to resurrect dead leads with a specific, non-desperate re-engagement strategy.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Pull leads that are 60 to 120 days old — recent enough to remember you, old enough that the objection may have resolved.
2. Look for a new reason to reach out — rate change, new carrier offering, market update.
3. Call or text with that specific new reason.
4. Do not apologize for reaching out after a long gap.
5. Ask one question about whether their situation has changed.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Hey Tom, this is Jason. We talked about your home and auto back in December. I know the timing was not right then. I wanted to reach out because there have been some rate changes with a carrier that I think would specifically benefit your profile. Has anything changed on your end since we talked?
Prospect: Actually yeah, I am ready to look at it again now.
Agent: Perfect. Let me pick up where we left off.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Calling dead leads with no new angle — same call gets the same result
- Apologizing for reaching out
- Treating the call like a brand new lead instead of a warm reconnect
- Not asking if anything has changed before re-pitching


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An outbound call to a lead from 90 days ago who got a quote but said the timing was not right at the time.

lessons.title: Quoted But Didn't Buy
lessons.content:
The quote is the opening, not the closing.


WHY THIS WORKS

A prospect who received a quote but did not buy is warmer than any cold lead you will ever work. They know you. They have information. They just have not made a decision. The quoted-but-did-not-buy follow-up is one of the highest-conversion activities you can do. This drill trains you to approach these prospects with a specific strategy that moves them from quote to decision.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Reference the specific quote — carrier, rate, coverage.
2. Give them one new piece of information or a resolution to what stopped them.
3. Be direct about the purpose of the call: 'I am calling to see if we can get this finalized.'
4. Ask what is still holding them back.
5. Handle the remaining objection and close.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Hey Karen — Jason here. I sent you the bundle quote last Thursday — $198 for home and auto. I wanted to follow up because I had one more carrier come back with a lower number. But more importantly — I want to know if there is anything about the quote itself that did not feel right, because I want to make sure you are in the right place before your renewal hits.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Calling to check in without referencing the specific quote
- Not asking what stopped them from moving forward
- Presenting the same quote with no new information
- Being apologetic or passive in the follow-up tone


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect received a quote five days ago and has not responded to the follow-up email. The agent is calling to re-engage.

lessons.title: Referral Ask After Bind
lessons.content:
The moment after the sale is your best referral opportunity.


WHY THIS WORKS

The moment right after a prospect becomes a client is the highest point of their satisfaction and trust. They feel good about the decision. They are in a positive emotional state. That is the perfect moment to ask for a referral — not weeks later when the feeling has faded. This drill trains you to ask for referrals naturally and specifically at the end of every sale.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Confirm the bind and congratulate them genuinely.
2. Transition to the referral ask naturally: 'Quick question before I let you go...'
3. Be specific: 'Is there anyone in your household or circle who owns a home and might be in a similar situation?'
4. If they give a name, get the contact information immediately.
5. If they hesitate, make it easier: 'You can just text me their name — no commitment on their end.'


EXAMPLE

Agent: You are all set — everything is confirmed and your documents will hit your email within the hour. Hey, quick question before I let you go — do you know anyone else, maybe a neighbor or family member, who owns a home and might be overpaying like you were?
Prospect: Actually my brother just bought a house.
Agent: Perfect. What is the best way to reach him? I promise to take care of him the same way I took care of you.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Waiting weeks after the sale to ask for a referral
- Asking too broadly: 'Do you know anyone?' — no one ever says yes to that
- Not asking for the contact information when they give a name
- Asking for a referral before the prospect feels fully satisfied with their purchase


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent just successfully bound a home and auto policy and is about to end the call. This is the referral ask drill.

lessons.title: Multi-Touch Follow-Up Sequence
lessons.content:
Fortune is in the fifth follow-up.


WHY THIS WORKS

Most sales require multiple contacts before a decision is made. The mistake agents make is giving up after one or two attempts. A strategic multi-touch sequence keeps you in front of a prospect without being annoying — because each touch adds new value instead of repeating the same ask. This drill teaches you to plan and execute a 5-touch follow-up sequence.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Touch 1 (same day): Specific follow-up referencing the call with next action.
2. Touch 2 (day 2): New information — rate update, carrier news, coverage insight.
3. Touch 3 (day 4): Different channel — if you called, now text or email.
4. Touch 4 (day 7): Value-add — market info, renewal tip, coverage checklist.
5. Touch 5 (day 14): Direct ask — 'I want to make sure I have not dropped the ball. Are you still looking?'


EXAMPLE

Agent: Day 7 touch: 'Hey Mark — sharing something I tell every homeowner this time of year. Most carriers file rate increases in Q1 — locking in now before the increase hits saves the difference. Worth a quick call this week?'


COMMON MISTAKES

- Using the same message across all five touches
- Giving up before touch 5
- Making every touch an ask instead of mixing in value-adds
- Not varying the channel across the sequence


PRACTICE SCENARIO

Planning and practicing a full 5-touch follow-up sequence for a prospect who got a quote but has gone quiet.

lessons.title: Pending Policy Follow-Up
lessons.content:
A verbal yes is not a bound policy. Stay on it.


WHY THIS WORKS

The gap between a verbal commitment and a bound policy is where deals die. Documents that do not get signed, payments that do not clear, underwriting questions that go unanswered — any of these can kill a deal that felt closed. This drill trains you to manage the pending period with the same energy you brought to the sale.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Set a clear expectation at the time of sale: what happens next and when.
2. Follow up on outstanding items before they become problems.
3. Check in within 24 hours of sending documents.
4. Be proactive about underwriting questions — do not wait for the carrier to chase the client.
5. Confirm the bind date and follow up to confirm the client received confirmation.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Hey Sandra — I submitted everything this morning. You should get an email from the carrier within a few hours to confirm. One quick thing — they may ask for a photo of your roof through their app. If that comes through, just complete it on your phone and it takes about two minutes. I will check back with you tomorrow to make sure everything cleared. Any questions in the meantime?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Treating a verbal yes as a done deal and moving on
- Not setting expectations about the pending process at the time of sale
- Waiting for the carrier to handle outstanding items without staying involved
- Not following up after documents are sent to confirm they were received


PRACTICE SCENARIO

An agent who just got a verbal commitment on a home policy. The application has been submitted and the agent needs to manage the pending period.

lessons.title: Pipeline Control & Prioritization
lessons.content:
Not all follow-ups are equal. Know which ones to run on.


WHY THIS WORKS

Pipeline control is about making smart decisions with your follow-up time. An agent who follows up on every lead equally is less effective than one who prioritizes ruthlessly. This drill trains you to score, sort, and prioritize your pipeline so you always know who to call first, who to nurture, and who to let go.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Score each lead: hot (quote given, ready to decide), warm (interested, timing issue), cold (no engagement in 30+ days).
2. Work hot leads first — every day, first hour.
3. Warm leads get the multi-touch sequence treatment.
4. Cold leads get a resurrection attempt once and then move to email only.
5. Set a hard cutoff — leads with no engagement after 90 days get a final attempt then archived.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Working through the pipeline — top three today: Lisa who got a quote Tuesday and said she needed to think, David who I have called twice with no answer, and Karen who is renewing in 8 days. Lisa gets a same-day call. Karen gets a urgency call today. David gets a text and a voicemail and moves to warm if there's no response.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Calling leads in the order they are listed instead of by priority
- Spending equal time on hot and cold leads
- Not setting a cutoff for leads that are going nowhere
- Letting the pipeline grow without cleaning it — creates a false sense of activity


PRACTICE SCENARIO

The agent has 20 open leads in their pipeline. This drill is about making smart prioritization decisions at the start of the work day.

courses.title: Call Control
courses.description: 8 drills for steering a call — redirecting a rambling prospect, controlling pace, handling price shoppers and competitor talk, and keeping momentum after an objection.

lessons.title: Redirecting A Rambling Prospect
lessons.content:
Let them talk. Then steer with one sentence.


WHY THIS WORKS

A prospect who goes off on tangents is not a problem — they are engaged. The mistake is either letting them talk indefinitely or cutting them off abruptly. The skill is to let them feel heard, acknowledge what they said genuinely, and use a bridge question to redirect back to the purpose of the call. Done well, the prospect does not even notice the redirect.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Let them finish — interrupting creates resistance.
2. Acknowledge what they said with one genuine sentence.
3. Use a bridge: 'That is actually relevant to what I want to ask you...' or 'Speaking of that...'
4. Ask a focused question that brings the conversation back on track.
5. Repeat as needed — some prospects need two or three bridges per call.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: ...and that is why I just don't trust insurance companies in general. My uncle had a terrible experience back in 2008 where they just...
Agent: That kind of experience changes how you look at the whole industry. What your uncle went through is actually exactly why I ask so many questions upfront — because the carrier you choose matters more than most people realize. Speaking of which — when was the last time you actually compared what you are getting versus what you are paying?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Cutting the prospect off mid-sentence — creates friction
- Letting them go so long that you lose control of the call timeline
- Not acknowledging what they said before redirecting — feels dismissive
- Redirecting to a completely unrelated topic — makes it obvious


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect who tends to go on tangents. The agent needs to keep the conversation on track without being rude.

lessons.title: Controlling Call Pace
lessons.content:
You set the pace. The prospect follows.


WHY THIS WORKS

Call pace is one of the least discussed but most important elements of a successful insurance call. Too fast and the prospect feels rushed and suspicious. Too slow and they check out or take control. The right pace is deliberate — you move quickly through low-value exchanges and slow down at high-value moments. This drill trains you to be intentional about pace throughout the call.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Move quickly through administrative questions — carrier, how long, basic details.
2. Slow down at discovery moments — pause after important questions, let silence work.
3. Slow down significantly at the recommendation — never rush the presentation.
4. Speed back up at the close — momentum is your friend at decision time.
5. Calibrate to the prospect — mirror and lead.


EXAMPLE

Agent: How long have you been with your current carrier?
Prospect: About seven years.
Agent: And have they reviewed your coverage in those seven years or has it just renewed automatically?
Prospect: Mostly just renewed.
Agent: [pause] That is actually the most important thing I want to spend a few minutes on today. A lot changes in seven years — home value, liability exposure, life changes — and most carriers do not automatically adjust to that. Let me show you what that means for your situation.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Rushing through the entire call at one uniform pace
- Slowing down at administrative questions that do not need it
- Rushing through the recommendation — the most important part of the call
- Not adjusting pace when the prospect signals they need more time


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A full mock call where the agent practices deliberate pace variation throughout all stages.

lessons.title: Transitioning From Rapport To Business
lessons.content:
The pivot from friendly to purposeful is where agents lose control.


WHY THIS WORKS

Getting into rapport is easy. Getting out of it and into business is where most agents struggle. The transition needs to feel natural, not abrupt. The best transitions use a bridge that acknowledges the rapport moment and connects it to the purpose of the call. A bad transition sounds like: 'Anyway, so about your insurance...' A good one sounds like an organic flow from one topic to the next.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Let the rapport moment complete naturally.
2. Use a transition that connects the personal to the professional.
3. Re-state the purpose of the call briefly.
4. Ask the first real discovery question.
5. The tone should shift from casual to engaged, not from warm to cold.


EXAMPLE

Agent: That is a great neighborhood — I have seen a lot of people get solid rates in that area actually. Speaking of which, before I pull up what we can do for you — quick question. Are you in the same situation as most people I talk to there, where the policy has just been auto-renewing without a real review?
Prospect: Yeah, that is pretty much it.
Agent: That is what I figured. Let's change that today.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Transitioning too abruptly — feels like the rapport was fake
- Never transitioning — the call stays in small talk and never gets to business
- Using a generic transition instead of connecting it to something specific they said
- Losing the warm tone when you shift to business — keep the rapport alive


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A call that opened with a strong rapport moment about the prospect's new home. The agent needs to transition naturally into discovery.

lessons.title: Cutting Off The Price Shopper
lessons.content:
If you let them anchor on price, you have already lost.


WHY THIS WORKS

A price shopper opens the call by asking for your cheapest rate. If you immediately quote the cheapest option, you have lost the conversation — you are now just a commodity. The price shopper drill trains you to interrupt the price-first frame and reset the conversation around value before any numbers are discussed.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. When they lead with 'What's your cheapest rate?' — do not answer it directly.
2. Redirect: 'The cheapest rate depends entirely on what you need covered. Let me ask you a couple of questions.'
3. Run your normal discovery.
4. Present value before price in your recommendation.
5. If they keep pushing for the cheapest option, be honest: 'The cheapest option is not always the right option. Here is why.'


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I just want to know what the lowest rate you can get me is.
Agent: I can get you the lowest rate available for your profile — but the lowest rate changes based on what you need covered. If I give you a number without knowing your situation, it will not be accurate. Give me three minutes, two questions, and I will give you the real number. Deal?
Prospect: Fine, go ahead.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Quoting the cheapest option immediately to keep them on the phone
- Arguing about why price should not be the focus
- Not having a crisp, confident response ready for the price-first opener
- Letting them control the conversation around price for the entire call


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect opens the call by asking what the cheapest rate the agent can offer is. The agent needs to reset the frame immediately.

lessons.title: Steering Away From Competitor Talk
lessons.content:
Never fight on their turf. Bring it back to yours.


WHY THIS WORKS

When a prospect starts comparing you to a competitor or defending a competitor's offer, engaging in a point-by-point debate is almost always a losing move. Your job is to acknowledge, redirect, and focus on what you can do rather than what the competitor cannot. This drill trains you to steer competitor conversations toward your strengths without attacking theirs.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Do not attack the competitor — it makes you look insecure.
2. Acknowledge the mention briefly: 'They are a known carrier.'
3. Redirect: 'Let me show you what the comparison looks like specifically for your profile.'
4. Focus on what differentiates your offer — service, coverage, carrier stability.
5. If the competitor offer is genuinely better — say so and move on. Honesty builds trust.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: Geico gave me a quote that is $30 cheaper.
Agent: They are competitive on auto — no question. Can I ask what coverage limits they quoted you?
Prospect: I am not sure exactly.
Agent: That is usually where the difference lives. A lot of times the lower rate has lower liability limits. Let me show you what you are getting in each quote line by line and you can decide which one actually makes more sense.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Badmouthing the competitor — creates defensiveness and looks unprofessional
- Getting drawn into a feature-by-feature debate you cannot win
- Ignoring the competitor mention entirely
- Not asking for the details of the competitor quote


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect mentions they have a lower quote from a competitor and wants to know why they should pay more.

lessons.title: Keeping Momentum After An Objection
lessons.content:
Handle it and keep moving. Do not let the air out of the call.


WHY THIS WORKS

The moment an objection lands, many agents pause, slow down, and inadvertently signal that the objection was a big deal. That pause kills momentum. The best handlers acknowledge quickly, answer efficiently, and immediately re-establish forward motion. The prospect should feel like the objection was handled so well that it was almost a non-event.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Acknowledge in one sentence — not a paragraph.
2. Answer efficiently — give the key point, not the full explanation.
3. Re-establish momentum immediately: ask a forward-moving question or make a statement that assumes forward progress.
4. Do not pause and wait for them to validate your answer.
5. Keep the energy of the call at the same level it was before the objection.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: I just feel like $185 is a lot.
Agent: I hear you. What you are getting for $185 here versus what you have now is significantly different coverage — specifically the liability limits and the loss-of-use protection that your current policy does not include. That said, let me show you the mid-tier option which brings it down to $165. Does that give you more room?


COMMON MISTAKES

- Over-explaining the answer to the objection — drains momentum
- Pausing too long after answering as if waiting for judgment
- Dropping your energy level after the objection
- Not re-closing after handling the objection


PRACTICE SCENARIO

Mid-presentation, the prospect raises a price objection. The agent needs to handle it cleanly and keep the call moving without losing energy.

lessons.title: Controlling The Close Sequence
lessons.content:
The close is not one moment. It is a sequence you control.


WHY THIS WORKS

Top producers think of the close as a sequence of micro-decisions that lead to the final commitment — not a single high-stakes moment. Each micro-decision is a small yes that builds toward the big yes. Controlling the close sequence means knowing what order to present decisions in, which decisions to drive and which to offer choice on, and how to keep forward momentum through each step.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Start with the easiest decisions first — coverage tier, payment method.
2. Move to the higher-commitment steps once the easy yeses are established.
3. Never present the hardest decision first.
4. Confirm each decision before moving to the next.
5. Treat the final commitment as the logical conclusion of the sequence, not a separate event.


EXAMPLE

Agent: Okay — so we have home and auto together, effective first of the month. Does monthly work for you or do you want the annual discount?
Prospect: Monthly.
Agent: Got it. And is this the primary address for the policy — 142 Oak Street?
Prospect: Yes.
Agent: Perfect. Let me get your banking information and we will have you active by end of day.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Leading with the biggest commitment — the full annual payment
- Asking for everything at once instead of one decision at a time
- Not confirming each decision before moving to the next
- Treating the close as one big ask instead of a series of small ones


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A prospect who has expressed interest and is ready to move forward. The agent needs to walk through the close sequence cleanly without losing them on any step.

lessons.title: Taking Back A Derailed Call
lessons.content:
Every call can be recovered. Most agents do not try.


WHY THIS WORKS

Calls get derailed — by interruptions, by emotional tangents, by aggressive price shopping, by competitor comparisons. Most agents ride the derailed call to a bad ending. This drill trains you to recognize when a call has gone off track and take specific action to recover it. The recovery is almost always a single, well-placed question that re-establishes purpose.


HOW TO RUN THIS DRILL

1. Recognize when the call has derailed — prospect is in control, off-topic, or emotional.
2. Do not fight for control loudly — interrupt with empathy, not volume.
3. Acknowledge where they are: 'It sounds like you have a lot on your plate.'
4. Re-establish purpose with one clear question: 'Can I ask — what would make this conversation worth your time today?'
5. Use their answer to re-direct the call.


EXAMPLE

Prospect: ...I just feel like every insurance company is the same. They all just take your money and disappear. I have talked to three agents this week and they all said the same things and...
Agent: I hear you — and honestly, that frustration makes complete sense given what you have described. Let me ask you one thing: what would one of those three agents have had to do differently for you to actually trust them?
Prospect: I guess just be straight with me. Stop with the sales stuff.
Agent: Fair enough. No sales stuff. Here is exactly what I have for your profile, what it costs, and what it covers. You decide.


COMMON MISTAKES

- Trying to talk over a derailed prospect instead of acknowledging their state
- Giving up on the call instead of attempting a recovery
- Recovering the call and then going back to the same approach that derailed it
- Not identifying what actually derailed the call before attempting recovery


PRACTICE SCENARIO

A call that started well but has derailed into a frustrated, trust-resistant prospect who is skeptical of agents in general.
